claim_reviews.rationale: Inputs and five sequential actions generalize across distinct workshops and explicitly seek work vs impression, producer vs holder, independent role evidence, both endpoints, bridge and pre-contact alternative. The work-level stopping rule is distinct from stricter individual-sheet and exchange thresholds; next anchor is a concrete different Puvirnituq work, 75-62, whose catalogue caption and image I inspected on PDF p. 37.

Original scanned catalogue PDF p. 33 visually identifies 69-62, Kenojuak, bilingual title and stonecut; p. 3 says production in 1962 and also refers to 1963 approved graphics, so distributor label, object date and release are properly separated. Existing Kinngait dataset record covers local experimental practice and does not identify a separate edition.

National Gallery accession 38038 records 1962, stonecut in black and yellow on japan paper and cooperative 1995 gift. Archived Lethbridge 1988.164 says 40/50. National Gallery 2000–01 annual report p. 15 identifies the film print and block in its collection without block accession. First Arts lot 20 says unnumbered proof and openly speculates as to the filmed sheet; related but unproven individual-sheet identity is appropriately deferred. Dimensions differ without common stated measurement basis.

Original catalogue names Kenojuak; Dyck pp. 198–199 and note 39 give Rhoda Kayakjuak’s translated dialogue and distinguish voice-over. Independent Dorset Fine Arts caption credits Lukta cutting while First Arts assigns cutting to Iyola and printing to Lukta. Record properly leaves exclusive credit unresolved, does not equate this filmed sheet with accession 38038, and identifies its reliance on a published frame and translation rather than asserting independent viewing.

Ikeda/Tiampo draft version 4 pp. 37–39, 53–54 quotes Hiratsuka’s own 1962 account, describes Houston learning the Japanese rubbing pad and separately references his dated 1958 travel note; pp. 53–54 and figures document locally made sealskin pad IV-C-3558, publicity image PA-94469 and Kananginak Pootoogook interview. CMH exhibition inventory independently identifies local tools and prints brought back. These are an archival and curatorial reconstruction with distinct types of evidence, not fully independent curatorial publications or direct inspection of every historical item. Support is for adapting a Japanese-style rubbing tool at workshop scope, not a complete workflow or tool use on a specified sheet.

CMH object entry 1957 Three Caribous stonecut predates 1958–59 Japanese trip; this is a control against making the visit the origin of Kinngait stonecut practice, not a claim that every later tool had an earlier form. Draft figure 27 identifies IV-C-3559 as the different Talluliyuk block. Historical graph edge is not proposed.

The original catalogue PDF pp. 35–37 surveys Puvirnituq experiments in 1961 and Tinkl’s 1962 role, and p. 37 illustrates and captions Leah Qumalu Sea Goddess no. 75-62. Shared publication supports a cataloguing/release association and does not by itself establish technological transmission.

limitations: The independent review saw the published film frame and translation, not the complete original film or the translator’s original email.

The 1958 Houston note, Hiratsuka’s Japanese original, 2009 interview recording, physical baren and printing matrix were not directly inspected. Workshop adaptation remains a source-grounded historical inference at limited scope.
The next Puvirnituq target is a starting point, not evidence of technological transfer. No historical dataset changes or new graph edges are proposed.
